name: Back extension / deadlift strength
summary: Posterior-chain lifting (deadlifts, back extensions) that looksmaxxers pair with posture goals; well-established strength training, but no trials on appearance.
lead: The deadlift is a strength exercise in which a weight is lifted from the ground to hip level and lowered again, most often with a barbell. It is one of the three powerlifting lifts and a signature strongman event. The back extension, also called hyperextension, strengthens the erector spinae muscles through arching the spine back from a bent-forward position, performed on a Roman chair, 45-degree bench or reverse-hyperextension machine or with no equipment.

name: Yoga for posture
summary: Postural yoga used for mobility and alignment; some evidence for back pain and stress, little direct testing on posture or looks.
lead: Yoga for posture refers to using yoga asanas (physical poses) to improve flexibility, strength and alignment. Modern postural yoga was developed in the early twentieth century, revived in the 1920s by teachers such as Yogendra and Kuvalayananda and spread by students of Tirumalai Krishnamacharya, including B.K.S. Iyengar, whose Light on Yoga (1966) helped popularise it worldwide.

name: Pilates
summary: Core-focused mind-body exercise system used for posture and tone; reviews find back-pain benefit comparable to other exercise, with little direct posture-appearance data.
lead: Pilates is a mind-body exercise system named for Joseph Pilates, who developed it in the first half of the twentieth century and called it Contrology. He said the idea arose during his World War I internment on the Isle of Man, and published Your Health (1934) and Return to Life Through Contrology (1945). It emphasises core stability, breathing, alignment and flexibility, performed on a mat or on apparatus such as the Reformer and Cadillac.

name: Feldenkrais Method
summary: Gentle somatic movement education aimed at body awareness and efficient movement; reviews find no conclusive evidence of medical benefit, and posture looks are untested.
lead: The Feldenkrais Method is a form of somatic education devised by Israeli physicist and judo expert Moshe Feldenkrais (1904-1984). Its two formats are Awareness Through Movement, verbally guided group lessons, and Functional Integration, hands-on individual sessions. Proponents claim it improves movement quality and awareness and repairs brain-body connections.

name: Rolfing / structural integration
summary: Ten-session fascial bodywork for posture and alignment; reviews find little good evidence for its claims.
lead: Rolfing, also called structural integration, is a form of manual bodywork developed by the biochemist Ida Rolf (1896-1979). Practitioners apply slow, sustained pressure to the body's connective tissue (fascia) combined with movement cues, with the stated aim of lengthening tissue and aligning the body with gravity . It is usually delivered as a series of ten sessions .
claims: Rolfing can permanently realign posture by releasing fascia
Rolfing relieves chronic pain and stress

name: Chiropractic adjustments
summary: Chiropractic spinal manipulation: some low-certainty benefit for back and neck pain, little evidence for posture or appearance claims.
lead: A chiropractic adjustment is a manual intervention, most often a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust, applied to the joints of the spine; chiropractors use "adjustment" for what clinical literature calls spinal manipulation . It is the core technique of chiropractic, a profession founded in the 1890s by D. D. Palmer .

name: Chiropractic BioPhysics (CBP) cervical lordosis
summary: Chiropractic traction and exercise system aiming to restore the neck curve; evidence is mostly from CBP-affiliated studies.
lead: Chiropractic BioPhysics (CBP) is a posture-focused chiropractic technique founded in 1980 by Donald Harrison, Deanne Harrison and Daniel Murphy. It uses mathematical models of ideal spinal curves, and combines adjustments, exercises and traction to try to restore them . Cervical lordosis, the natural forward curve of the neck, is one of its main targets.

name: Physiotherapy for posture
summary: Supervised corrective exercise for posture; general physio is well established, posture-for-looks evidence is thin.
lead: Physiotherapy for posture refers to supervised exercise, manual therapy and education from a licensed physical therapist aimed at changing habitual alignment such as forward head posture or rounded shoulders . Physical therapy is a regulated healthcare profession that treats movement limitations, with exercise as a core tool .
claims: Physiotherapy exercises can be done alone at home instead of attending sessions

name: Postural Restoration Institute (PRI)
summary: Therapist-taught breathing and asymmetry exercise system for posture; little published trial evidence.
lead: Postural Restoration is a posture-based approach to physical medicine developed by physical therapist Ron Hruska in the early 1990s. In 1999 he founded the Postural Restoration Institute in Lincoln, Nebraska, to train health professionals . It uses manual and non-manual exercises to reposition and retrain the body toward neutral alignment .

name: Kinesiology tape posture taping
summary: Elastic tape across the upper back as a shoulder-position reminder; the tape's pain evidence is thin and posture-for-looks is untested.
lead: Kinesiology tape posture taping is the use of stretchy, adhesive elastic tape, commonly sold as Kinesio tape or K-tape, across the shoulders and upper back to cue a more upright shoulder position. In looksmaxxing and posture circles it is discussed as a way to counter rounded shoulders and forward-head posture, which people link to a more favorable side profile and neck line.

name: Dry needling / acupuncture
summary: Needling of tight muscles by clinicians; some short-term pain evidence, nothing for looks.
lead: Dry needling is a technique in which a thin solid needle is inserted into muscle, most often at myofascial trigger points, to treat muscle pain. It is distinct in theory from acupuncture, though the two use similar needles and the relationship is disputed between professions .

name: Cervical traction
summary: Neck pulling devices used in physio for nerve-root pain; no evidence for posture looks.
lead: Cervical traction is the application of a pulling force to the neck, in a clinic or with a home device, intended to relieve pressure on spinal structures. Physical therapists use it mainly for neck pain with nerve root symptoms such as cervical radiculopathy .

name: Spinal decompression therapy
summary: Computerized table traction for disc pain; small trials for back pain, nothing for looks.
lead: Non-surgical spinal decompression therapy is a table-based form of traction, usually computerized, offered by chiropractors and physical therapists for disc herniation and radiculopathy. The term spinal decompression also covers surgeries such as microdiscectomy and laminectomy that relieve pressure on nerves .

name: Ergonomic setup (monitor at eye level)
summary: Raising the screen to keep the head upright; sensible ergonomics, untested for looks.
lead: An ergonomic desk setup with the monitor at eye level is a posture practice in which people raise the screen so the head stays upright rather than tilting down. In posture and looksmaxxing communities it is described as a way to avoid so-called tech neck, a forward-head position associated with the neck and jawline.

name: Phone at eye level / tech neck avoidance
summary: Keeping the phone high to avoid head-down posture; tech neck itself lacks an agreed definition.
lead: Holding a phone at eye level to avoid tech neck, also called text neck, is a posture habit meant to prevent the head-down, forward-head position associated with prolonged device use. In looksmaxxing and posture communities it is linked to neck posture and jawline appearance.

name: Barefoot / minimalist shoes
summary: Thin, flat, wide-toed shoes marketed as restoring natural foot function; evidence for foot strength is emerging, evidence for looks or posture is absent.
lead: Barefoot or minimalist shoes are footwear designed to approximate walking or running barefoot. A 2015 consensus definition describes them as causing minimal interference with the natural movement of the foot, and a 2018 paper proposed objective criteria of a sole and upper weighing 200 g or less, a heel height of 20 mm or less and a heel-to-toe drop of 7 mm or less. Common features are a thin flexible sole, zero or near-zero drop, no arch support and a toe box wider than in conventional shoes; Vibram FiveFingers, Merrell Glove and Xero Prio are cited examples.
claims: Conventional shoes squeeze the toes and cause deformities like bunions and plantar fasciitis; wide toe boxes fix this.
Better foot mechanics from barefoot shoes improve posture and make you look better.
Barefoot shoes improve lifting performance and squat form.

name: Sleeping without a pillow
summary: Resting the head flat on the mattress, pitched online as a fix for forward head posture; comfort and sleeping position decide the outcome and direct evidence is thin.
lead: Sleeping without a pillow is the practice of resting the head directly on a mattress or other flat surface, with no head support or elevation. Some people reach it gradually by reducing the height of a thin pillow or folded towel over time. Accounts trace the idea in part to Joseph Pilates, who advised lying flat on a firm surface without a pillow in his book Return to Life Through Contrology.
claims: Sleeping without a pillow reduces forward head posture.
It is good for the spine and neck.

name: Chestmaxxing / chest-out posture
summary: Holding the chest open and raised as a posture habit; no studies of it as an appearance tactic, though open posture is generally read as confident.
lead: Chestmaxxing or chest-out posture refers to carrying the chest open and raised as part of a posture-focused approach to appearance. Sources specific to the term are very limited.

name: Posture Botox / muscle relaxants
summary: Injecting botulinum toxin into neck or trapezius muscles for tension; established for some neck conditions, untested as a posture or looks tool.
lead: Posture Botox refers to the use of botulinum toxin injections in neck or trapezius muscles for tension. Botulinum toxin is an acetylcholine release inhibitor that causes flaccid paralysis of the injected muscle, with the effect slowly reversing as the nerve regenerates.

name: Scoliosis bracing / fusion surgery
summary: Established orthopaedic treatments for spinal curvature; bracing aims to halt progression in growing teens, fusion straightens severe curves.
lead: Bracing and spinal fusion are the two main treatments for progressive scoliosis. Bracing is used only while a patient is still growing, aiming to stop the curve progressing to the point where surgery is needed. Surgery is usually recommended for curves likely to progress beyond about 45 to 50 degrees, for curves interfering with breathing or sitting, and for curves that would be cosmetically unacceptable in adulthood.

name: Posture tracker wearable (Upright Go)
summary: A small sensor that vibrates when you slouch; used in several clinician ergonomics studies, with no study of it as a looks tool.
lead: UpRight Go 2 is a commercially available wearable posture-training device that records neck and spine posture and provides biofeedback to prompt correction. It is promoted for slouching, and the entry is discussed here as posture gear.

name: Neck hammock / cervical stretcher
summary: Over-door neck traction harness borrowed from physical therapy; sold for posture, but research covers neck pain, not looks.
lead: A neck hammock, also sold as an over-the-door cervical traction device, is a home product that uses a head harness, straps and a pulley or door mount to apply a pulling force along the neck. It is a consumer version of cervical traction, a technique used in physical therapy to separate the neck vertebrae and stretch soft tissue.

name: Lacrosse ball / massage gun
summary: Self-massage tools for muscle tension; research is limited to recovery and mobility, with nothing on looks.
lead: A lacrosse ball is a firm rubber ball used for self-massage against a wall or floor, and a massage gun is a handheld battery-powered percussive device that delivers rapid pulses, commonly 20 to 60 Hz, through interchangeable heads. Both are used for muscle tension, soreness and trigger-point release.
claims: A massage gun can reduce facial asymmetry
Bonesmashing with a massage gun changes facial bones

name: Lumbar support cushion / seat wedge
summary: Chair add-ons for lumbar curve and pelvic tilt; the only study is a tiny pilot-seat trial for back pain, not looks.
lead: A lumbar support cushion is a pad placed between the lower back and a chair backrest to support the inward curve of the lumbar spine. A seat wedge is a tapered cushion that tilts the pelvis forward. Both are sold as chair add-ons for sitting posture and back comfort.

name: Kneeling or balance-ball chair
summary: Alternative seating meant to keep the spine upright; small studies look at lumbar curve, not looks.
lead: A kneeling chair supports the user with a sloped seat and padded shin rests so the thighs angle downward, opening the hip angle. A balance-ball chair uses an inflated exercise ball as the seat. Both are marketed as active seating that encourages upright posture.

name: Treadmill desk
summary: Walk-while-you-work setup; trials show more movement and small weight changes, not posture or looks.
lead: A treadmill desk is a computer desk adapted so the user walks slowly on a treadmill while working. It is intended to reduce sitting time and raise energy expenditure above resting levels, not to deliver aerobic exercise.

name: Roman chair / hyperextension bench
summary: A padded bench for back extensions that loads the spinal erectors; popular in posture and back-training routines, with little appearance-specific research.
lead: A Roman chair, also called a hyperextension bench, is exercise equipment that supports the body while the user performs movements aimed mainly at the lower back, and also the buttocks, hamstrings and abdominal muscles .

name: Inversion table
summary: A tilting frame for hanging upside down, used for back traction and by height-curious forum users; any height change is described as temporary and reports of serious injury exist.
lead: An inversion table is a device that secures the legs and tilts the user partly or fully upside down. It is a tool of inversion therapy, a form of spinal traction in which the body hangs at an inverted angle; gravity boots are another device used for this .
claims: Using an inversion table can add inches of height.
Glucosamine could lock in the height gained from inversion.
Inversion is safe for everyone to try.

name: In-office professional bleaching
summary: Dentist-applied high-concentration peroxide whitening in a single visit; produces visible shade change, with common sensitivity and fading over months.
lead: In-office professional bleaching is tooth whitening carried out by a dentist or hygienist using a high-concentration peroxide gel. The active agents are hydrogen peroxide and carbamide peroxide, which releases hydrogen peroxide on contact with water; the peroxide produces free radicals that break down pigment molecules so teeth reflect less light .

name: Dentist take-home whitening trays
summary: Custom-fitted trays loaded with dentist-supplied peroxide gel and worn at home; gentler on sensitivity than in-office bleaching, with modest shade gains.
lead: Dentist take-home whitening trays are custom-fitted trays, made from an impression of the teeth, that hold peroxide gel against the teeth while worn at home. Carbamide peroxide, which releases hydrogen peroxide on contact with water, is the usual agent .
